questions.question: What is the difference between exported and unexported identifiers in Go?
questions.title: Exported Vs Unexported
questions.direct_answer: Capitalized names are exported (public — visible to importing packages). Lowercase are unexported (package-private). One rule, no keywords — the ONLY visibility boundary in Go.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: Capitalized names are exported (public — visible to importing packages). Lowercase are unexported (package-private). One rule, no keywords — the ONLY visibility boundary in Go.

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
The rule, verified:

```go
package math

func Add(a, b int) int { return a + b }  // exported
func internalHelper() int { ... }            // unexported — importing packages can't see it
var Count int                                // exported variable
const maxRetries = 3                          // unexported constant
type Config struct { ... }                    // exported type
```

An importing package: math.Add works; math.internalHelper is a compile error — undefined.

The rule's scope: it applies uniformly — functions, types, methods, fields, constants, variables, packages' interfaces. The identifier's first character IS the visibility. No public/private/protected keywords; no package hierarchy (Go's packages are flat — no subpackage inheritance).

The design consequence: package APIs are DESIGNED by what you capitalize. The exported surface is the contract; everything else is implementation. Reviewers read a Go package's API by listing its exported identifiers — no separate interface file to maintain.

The conventional pair: an exported function with an unexported helper (the exported one is the stable API; the helper can change freely). Testing still reaches unexported names via the _test.go same-package access — the topic covered earlier.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    CAP[Name — Capitalized] --> EXP[exported — importable]
    LC[name — lowercase] → UNP[unexported — package-only]
    UNP → TEST[_test.go same package: still visible]
    UNP → JSON[invisible to encoding/json]
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
The selector mechanics: the compiler resolves x.Name where the name starts uppercase → find it in the package's export data (the compiled .a file includes only exported identifiers). Unexported names are absent from the export data — the import literally can't reference them, not just 'isn't allowed.' That's why the error is undefined rather than access-denied.

The JSON interplay — the common surprise: encoding/json uses ONLY exported fields. A struct with all unexported fields marshals to {}. The tags can't rescue an unexported field. The DTO pattern (exported wire-type vs unexported domain-type) exists because of this intersection.

The interface satisfaction interaction: a method with an exported name satisfies interfaces across packages; unexported methods only satisfy same-package interfaces. This enables the sealed-interface pattern (an interface with an unexported method can only be satisfied within the package — the marker method technique for closed type hierarchies).
